response.consequence: In credential-sync mode, refreshing a token overwrites the stored refresh_token with the string "refresh_token". It also stores a NaN expiry_date. The next refresh then fails and the integration breaks until the user reconnects.
response.explanation: z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() both return "[object Object]", because Zod schemas don't override toString. The two computed keys are therefore the same, and the second (z.unknown().optional()) overwrites the first (z.number()). The schema is effectively {access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown optional}. z.object strips unknown keys by default. In credential-sync mode, a payload like {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in} parses successfully, but the returned data holds only access_token. The expires_in and refresh_token fields are dropped, and the intended "any number property is the expiry" rule is never enforced. The code at line 26 then sees no refresh_token and writes the literal placeholder "refresh_token". Callers such as zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:119-124 copy newTokens.refresh_token into the stored key, and compute newTokens.expires_in * 1000, which is NaN because expires_in is undefined. They then persist both to the DB.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema collapses to one "[object Object]" key and strips real token fields

response.consequence: Timing-based recovery of the shared secret is theoretically possible and would let an attacker overwrite any user's app credentials. Malformed requests produce 500 responses and server error noise rather than clean 4xx responses.
response.explanation: The unset-secret bypass does not happen. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED (packages/lib/constants.ts:103) is truthy only when both CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are set, and the handler returns 403 before the secret check otherwise. So `undefined === undefined` and the empty-string decrypt key cannot be reached. Two weaker defects remain. (1) The secret is compared with `!==` at lines 23-26, which is not constant-time, so a remote caller could in principle recover it through timing. If the header is sent twice, Node gives an array, which never equals the secret; that case is safe. (2) `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` at line 29 is not caught. Neither are `JSON.parse` or `symmetricDecrypt` at lines 56-58. A malformed body, or keys that fail to decrypt, throws an unhandled error and the caller gets a 500 instead of a 400.
response.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`; invalid bodies are not handled

response.consequence: On a misconfigured deployment, an unauthenticated caller can create or overwrite any user's app credentials through this endpoint. That includes replacing OAuth tokens for any user.
response.explanation: The handler compares `req.headers[name] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` with no check that the secret is configured. If APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true but CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, a request with no secret header has `undefined` on both sides. The `!==` is then false and the request is treated as authenticated. The comparison is also not constant-time. The handler goes on to write arbitrary `key` JSON into the credential of any userId, and the decryption key falls back to an empty string.

other_findings.consequence: With credential sync enabled, every token refresh through parseRefreshTokenResponse throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Zoom and Office365 calendar then fail to refresh. Office365 silently drops the new tokens, because the `success &&` spread yields nothing.
other_findings.explanation: The schema keys are `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. These evaluate to a fixed stringified-object key (likely "[object Object]"), not a wildcard. Both entries also collapse to one key, so the schema requires a numeric property with that literal name. Real token responses lack it, so safeParse fails whenever credential sharing and the sync endpoint are both enabled. The `.passthrough()` the comment implies is missing as well. The expiry is never actually checked.
other_findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses bogus computed keys and can never validate real responses

other_findings.consequence: The stored credential's real refresh token is replaced by the bogus string. Any later refresh that does not go through the sync endpoint fails with invalid_grant.
other_findings.explanation: When the response has no refresh_token, the parser sets it to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers such as Office365 calendar merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential.
other_findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token written over missing refresh token

response.consequence: With sharing enabled, token refresh fails for axios-based and SDK-based apps. In hubspot it can overwrite the stored credential with a corrupt value. Anyone who can reach the sync endpoint can request tokens for a given user id and app slug, because the request carries no authentication.
response.explanation: When credential sharing is enabled, the helper returns the raw fetch Response. It sends no auth header or secret, and it never checks response.ok. The non-sync branch returns whatever the refresh callback returns, which is an axios response in zohocrm and bigin and a parsed token object from the SDK in hubspot. zohocrm reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`, and a fetch Response has no `.data`, so that line throws a TypeError. hubspot assigns the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn` and `.accessToken`, which are undefined on a Response. It then writes that Response to the credential key. Error statuses (401/500) are never detected.
response.title: Sync branch returns raw fetch Response, unauthenticated and unchecked, breaking callers

response.consequence: Constructing the Salesforce calendar service fails on every call, so the Salesforce integration breaks. Even with the import added, the connection would still use the stale access token.
